One consequence is visible in the asylum data. In Q1 of FY2026, IJs issued 3,250 asylum grants and 21,309 denials, with 22,106 applications deemed "abandoned." Including abandonments in the denominator produces a grant rate of about 7%, a historic low for the immigration courts.

The White House framed the overhaul in an April 10 statement titled "Era of Amnesty Is Over." EOIR director Daren Margolin described the goal as reducing the backlog and "unwinding the policies of the Biden administration."

Two of the judges fired April 10 (Roopal Patel and Nina Froes) had ruled against the deportation of pro-Palestinian students Rümeysa Öztürk and Mohsen Mahdawi. Patel told GBH News she "could have ruled either way in that case and probably would have still ended up fired."

The legal footing shifted in March 2026, when the Merit Systems Protection Board ruled that the attorney general may fire immigration judges at will, classifying them as "inferior officers" of the executive branch.

For scale: EOIR had about 650 immigration judges on staff at the end of FY2023. Removing and replacing 113 in roughly 15 months is not routine personnel management. Before this administration, probationary dismissals of immigration judges were rare.

According to the National Association of Immigration Judges, 113 immigration judges have been fired or forced out since January 2025, with six terminated over a single weekend earlier this month. Alongside 140 new hires, that's a near-total turnover of the bench. 🧵

On deportations: ICE is on track for roughly 440,000 removals in FY2025. Using consistent metrics, the increase over the last Biden fiscal year is smaller than the rhetoric suggests though the FY2026 pace has clearly accelerated.

I also get asked often whether the official death count is trustworthy. People who die inside facilities are likely counted. People released in deteriorating health, discharged from hospitals, or who die after deportation almost certainly are not.

That rural geography compounds the medical crisis. When someone is seizing on the floor for an hour before an ambulance arrives, the nearest adequate emergency care is a real, measurable distance away.

Winn sits in what some of us call "detention alley" in rural Louisiana. Private contractors seek out cheap land in compliant communities, and the economic incentive to host a facility tends to outweigh scrutiny of what happens inside.

When journalists and independent physicians have reviewed the full records behind these deaths, they keep finding the same pattern: delayed responses, ignored medical complaints, and emergency care that arrived too late or never arrived at all.
